subject: convoyHauler
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: armoured convoy hauler guarding a sealed cargo pod.
Style: low-poly cyberpunk.
reasoning:
I'm planning a low-poly cyberpunk armoured convoy hauler as a single TypeScript module, designing a heavy multi-wheeled truck with an angular cab guarding a sealed cargo pod.

Thinking through the rig: a chassis root with wheel joints for spin, steering joints on the front axle, and turret yaw/pitch joints for the roof-mounted autocannon. I'm sketching dimensions—roughly 9m long, 2.8m wide, 3.8m tall with the pod, six wheels across three axles (steering front, tandem rear)—to block out the cab, flatbed, and pod placement.

Now I'm working out the actual layout: body spanning about 9.6m in length, 2.8m wide, with wheel hubs at radius 0.62 placed outward near the frame rails, and a cab section sloping forward into the nose. I'm considering using a loft operation to build the hull shape, feeding it station points along the length with varying width and height to get the sloped hood and body profile, though I still need to figure out how the loft's cross-section is defined.

Given the 64 flat color limit, I'm planning out the vehicle's palette and paint scheme, starting with a dark gunmetal hull using a panelled paint for plating texture.

Now I'm defining accent colors—thinking between hazard yellow or a cyberpunk magenta/cyan combo against a deep indigo-slate hull. I'm also sketching the cargo pod as a lathed capsule shape with rounded ends and low-poly segments.

I'm detailing the pod further: hazard-striped banding via paint masks, a pale ceramic body with neon seam lines, a glowing cyan seal window, warning decals, strap/clamp fastenings, and a lock with a glowing red status light, all resting on cradle supports with specific position and length values along the bed.

Now I'm working out the lathe profile for the pod shape, defining its radius points along the axis to create a rounded capsule form with octagonal cross-section segments for a low-poly look.

For coloring, I'm setting up a paint function based on position along the outline—pale base color with hazard stripe patterns near the ends using a diagonal stripe formula, plus darker shading toward the bottom for a worn, weathered look.

I'm planning decals for the pod surface: a corporate logo plus "SEALED / BIO-HAZARD / UNIT 7" lettering rendered as SVG text, applied onto the pod part since it supports decal targeting. I'm also adding three ring bands as torus shapes positioned along the pod's length to break up the surface detail.

Now I'm adding a hexagonal cylinder seal lock near the rear with a glowing red ring and cyan status bar, plus hold-down straps that loop around the pod's circumference at a given height, using surface loop sampling to get the contour before sweeping a strap shape along it.

Now I'm working on the saddle cradle blocks under the pod, then moving to the chassis structure—frame rails, crossmembers, fuel tanks, battery, exhaust, and the deck plating with panel detailing. I'm also sketching out wheel arch fenders using an extruded arc profile positioned at the sides.

Designing wheel geometry next...

Designing the wheel hub assembly: a gunmetal rim plate, eight lug bolts, a glowing cyan neon torus ring that spins with the wheel, and a hexagonal central hub cap, all positioned on the outer face of the tire.

Each wheel gets around six merged parts for roughly thirty-six total. For joints, I'm setting up the chassis spine root and steering joints for the front axle, giving them the hinge orientation needed so steering rotates around the vertical axis while the wheel still spins independently.

For the wheel spin joint, I want rotation about the axle, so I'll orient the bone along the axle direction (dir [s,0,0]) and let its own Y-axis rotation drive the wheel spin, while the steering joint uses a vertical bone direction so it rotates about world Y.

For non-steered wheels I'll skip the suspension joint and parent the spin joint directly to the chassis to keep things simple, and I'll use role "hinge" for these wheel joints since that fits the recognized rigger role list better than inventing a new category.

Now I'm working out wheel placement and axle spacing—deciding whether to use four axles with front steering, checking that wheel diameter (about 1.24) leaves enough clearance between mid and rear axles, and sketching approximate z-positions along the chassis so the fenders and cab fit without overlap.

Mapping out the cab's angular wedge shape — a cab-over armored nose with a sloped front bumper, raised hood line, and the joint where the hood meets the windshield.

Now I'm working out the sloped windshield geometry: it's a slanted slit face running from the nose peak up to the roofline, and I need to compute the angle and outward normal of that face so I can place a tilted glass pane flush against it.

Working out the rotation angle needed so the panel's local axes align with the face's up/back direction, then thinking about writing a reusable helper function that computes this slope and builds a tilted glass box with the correct orientation and thickness.

Still working out normal direction...

I'll settle on consistent outward-normal convention: traversing front-bottom up, over the roof, and down the back always gives correct outward orientation. Now I'm designing a reusable `facePlate` helper that takes a bone, two profile points, width, thickness, offset, color, and UV, so I can apply it uniformly to sloped armor like the windshield, hood, and side plates.

Given the scope of this build (~250 parts, 5-8 textures), I need to plan the texture budget carefully: a corporate logo for the pod, a hazard warning label ("SEALED CARGO / LOT 7-ΩX / DO NOT OPEN"), a cab door badge reading "CV-07", a status screen texture with bars and graphs for the dash, and a tinted windscreen visor texture with gradient reflections and a slit grill pattern, plus headlight detailing.

I'm also mapping out additional decal textures: a grille mesh for the nose intake, a rear license plate, graffiti-style tag decals and side stripe chevron livery, a radiation/bio symbol for the pod end cap, and warning triangle stickers. For applying these I'm deciding between curved decals on the pod versus flat plane geometry for other surfaces, working out how each plane's facing direction and orientation needs to align so the texture draws correctly on cab sides versus front faces.

Working through the cross product for the viewing direction, I realize that from the viewer's position looking along -X, the right vector resolves to -Z, meaning the truck's nose points toward the left of the image -- so any text decals on that side will read tail-ward rather than nose-first.

For the opposite side (-X direction decal), the orientation flips naturally so text reads toward the nose as expected. I'm also keeping the color palette constrained to roughly 20 flat colors across textures to stay well under limits.

Now I'm sketching out the cab construction: a hull-painted body extrusion with panel detailing, roof armor slabs, a round roof hatch, a turret with yaw/pitch joints for the autocannon, plus antennas, a sensor dome, and a light bar.

Rounding out the design with sloped windscreen glass, slit visors, glowing teal side windows, angled armored shutters, a nose bull-bar with spiked bumper teeth, white-cyan headlight slits, magenta under-glow neon strips along the skirt, a winch with tow hooks, a cab step, grab rail, and camera-pod mirrors. I'm weighing whether to add hinged door joints too, but deciding to skip them to keep the joint count manageable alongside wheels, steering, turret, and hatch rigs.

I'm now working through the frame details — chassis rails, crossbeams, drive axle rods, diff pumpkin, springs, side skirt armor slats, and mudflaps — then figuring out exact placement for twin exhaust stacks behind the cab, calculating clearances against the pod's rounded end cap so the stacks fit cleanly in the gap without overlapping.

I'm also planning the rear of the vehicle: an armored bumper, red neon tail lights, license plate, a sealed pod rear cap, rear ladder/ramp, tow hitch, fuel tank, and spare tire. For the deck, I'm sizing the paneled box and side rail walls, deciding wall height and thickness to match the body proportions.

Checking the deck height against wheel clearance, I realize the wheels poke slightly past the deck edges, so I'm raising the deck up and adding fender arches over the wheels so they fit properly, then working out where the chassis frame rails sit underneath.

Simplifying instead: cab lower body bottom at y=1.35 with wheels peeking out beneath, fenders flaring at x±1.2 to partially cover the wheel width without fully enclosing them.

Now I'm tracing the cab outline as a series of points going from front-bottom, up the sloped nose, over the roof, down the back, and along the bottom, setting coordinates for a slightly angled front face and rounded nose top.

Still plotting hull points...

I'll set detail to about 0.34 for roughly one chamfer step, confirming it only affects extrusion. The outline bevel should work fine even with concave corners since it shrinks to fit.

Now I'm planning the surface details: window slit, door seams with panel paint, badge decals, livery stripe, handle, armored hood vents, and a glowing hood strip. For the roof, I'm positioning a turret mount with a ring, yaw/pitch joints, an autocannon barrel with shroud, ammo box, and a glowing red sensor eye.

I'm sizing the turret barrel to point forward over the hood, bringing overall vehicle height to around 4.0 units — tall but fitting for an armored hauler. I'm also adding a roof sensor mast with a spinning amber beacon, plus underglow strips along the underbody between the axles in magenta and cyan tones for a neon accent look.

Now I'm defining the full color palette: dark gunmetal tones, steel grays, pod white/gray shades, hazard yellow, magenta, cyan, red, amber, white, rubber black, and a glowing teal glass tint, which I'll use to assign paint materials across the model.

Writing hull shader logic...

Writing hazard stripe paint for bumpers using a checkerboard pattern based on position, then starting on the main code imports and helper setup.

I'm defining a helper that attaches parts to the chassis bone by default rather than relying on nearest-joint inference, since that could incorrectly bind to a wheel joint. I'll also add a mirror helper to duplicate symmetric parts across both sides.

Now I'm sketching out the overall build function structure with the builder setup and return value, then thinking about texture resolution — the truck's painted surface area is large enough that the default paint size would blur the fine panel seams, so I'm bumping it up to 2048 to preserve that detail.

Even at the higher resolution, 2.5mm seams would still blur, so I'm deciding to write a custom plating paint function with thicker seams (about 1.5cm) rather than relying on built-in seam widths. Writing custom seam logic...

Now I'm defining vehicle constants like wheel radius and axle positions along the z-axis, with front axles marked steerable, plus the chassis joint position for the spine.

Adding wheel and steering joints...

Now I'm thinking through the remaining joints: turret pitch and yaw, roof hatch hinge, beacon spin, and whether to include cab doors with window and handle details on the side panels.

I'll add a slightly proud door panel with a window slit, handle, and neon edge trim, painted in a lighter hull tone. Now I'm moving into coding the actual parts, starting with the frame and underbody rails positioned alongside the wheel hubs.

Adding crossmembers, axles, differential pumpkins, and leaf springs...

Simplifying to two leaves per stack instead of three brings the count down to a more manageable 40 parts. For the fuel tanks, I'm placing cylinders along the rails between axle 2 and axle 3, sizing them to fit the free space in that gap and rotating them to run lengthwise along z.

I'm also planning a coolant tank and glowing cyan battery pack on the opposite side for visual contrast, plus angled side skirts between the wheels -- though I need to double check the skirt's vertical placement since it currently overlaps with the tank geometry under the deck.

For the deck itself, I'm laying out the main plated hull box with its length and center position tuned so the top sits flush at the target height, leaving room on the sides for optional rail details, which I'll skip in favor of simpler tool-box details.

Now I'm positioning toolbox lockers along the deck edges near the wheel fenders, which arch up over the wheels and rise to meet the deck's underside, and figuring out where additional lockers fit between the axles relative to where the pod's lower octagonal profile intersects the deck.

Checking fender positions confirm lockers clear the deck safely, so I'll place them at two spots along the side plus a spare tyre rack at the rear. For the cradle supports under the pod, I'm sketching saddle blocks at a few z-positions, but realize they'd intersect the pod's bottom curve near the octagon's center, so I need to rethink the deck height relationship there.

Now I'm working out the saddle geometry as angled wedge chocks on either side where the pod meets the deck tangentially, then shifting to defining the pod itself as a lathed shape with a specific profile curve, axis, and segment count to get the right rounded hull form.

For the pod's paint function, I'm using local model z-coordinates to apply hazard banding near the ends and blending base colors based on surface normal for lighting, while planning panel seam rings and longitudinal divisions...

Writing pod paint shader...

Still defining hazard striping...

I'm adding a magenta accent band near the middle, then setting up steel-colored ring bands with thin cyan glow torus accents at specific z positions around the pod.

I'm reconsidering the ring placement at three z-levels for a sealed-line glow effect, but realizing the torus segment count doesn't match the lathe's polygon sides, which could cause the rings to clip slightly into the surface since torus vertices sit outside the lathe's flat-faceted radius.

Settling on torus radius 1.08 with 0.03 tube for minimal sinking, then moving on to planning two strap sweeps with a buckle detail at the top, plus logo decals placed on both sides of the pod using mirrored x-direction offsets.

For the label decal, I'm reasoning through orientation so text reads correctly from the viewer's perspective on each side, then placing an end cap seal lock near the rear of the piece.

For the rear cap itself, I'm laying out a hex lock cylinder, a glowing red warning ring, a biohazard decal facing outward, plus latch bolts and a sealed indicator lamp. Then I'm planning the front cap with a keypad panel and status screen, positioned to leave a gap facing the cab.

Now I'm designing a thick glowing umbilical hose connecting the cab to the pod's front cap, plus top-mounted vents, an amber spinning hazard beacon, and cargo carry rails, before working out placement for side hatch panels with hex latches, logos, and a status screen decal.

I'm also outlining the cab's rounded body shape using a set of (z,y) coordinate points to define its bevel and silhouette, treating it as a centered extrusion with bone-like chassis geometry.

For the windscreen, I'm figuring out a glass band spanning the nose-to-roof edge, computing endpoints along that segment to position the facePlate with proper offset and thickness.

For the visor glass, I'm using a textured box geometry so the drawn SVG texture (gradient, reflection streaks, glowing HUD lines) wraps correctly onto the outward-facing surface, matching the box's local +Z axis orientation.

I'm adding a glow effect at moderate strength so the dark glass stays dark while the HUD lines read as teal glow bars, then setting the material to pure white so the texture's own colors show through unmodified.

Now I'm sketching the brow plate above the visor as a thicker box for a hazard-eyebrow look, and planning the slit side windows on the cab, positioning them to respect the windscreen's forward slope.

Working through the math for the window's vertical and depth bounds, I settle on a dark glass color with a subtle teal glow, deciding dark glass with a faint cyan reflection reads better than a strong glow.

Now I'm planning the door geometry: it's hinged at the front edge, spans a defined height and depth range, and contains its own window glass, frame, handle, grill vent, and a decal plane. I'm also laying out the cab roof with an armor plate, ribs, and a hinged hatch section.

I'm adding roof details next: a turret ring with yaw joint, a rotating turret body with an angled shield and pitch-jointed twin autocannon weapon, plus sensor domes, antennae whips, and a front light bar with amber glow strips.

Now I'm detailing the gun barrels and shrouds with muzzle brakes and ammo drums, checking the geometry so the barrels clear the hood and nose, then placing a front grille plane on the nose face with a hex-mesh glowing texture.

I'm also designing the ram bumper with hazard paint and spikes, headlights and fog lamps on the nose, plus tow hooks and a winch, while fine-tuning the grille plane's z-position to sit just outside the nose's beveled edge.

Now I'm shaping the hood with slanted vents and an intake box, then working out wheel arch geometry using inner and outer arc radii positioned over the front fenders.

The ring sector base sits at hub height, with the arch thickness around 0.62 and the arc covering the upper half as a mudguard hoop, fitting below the deck with the visible portion clear of the cab. I'll keep the outline polygonal with eight segments, color the fender with HULL2, and consider adding mudflaps behind the wheel.

Now I'm adding the rear details: dark boxes behind the rear axle wheels, a rear bumper box near z=-5, vertical red tail light strips glowing at either side, a brake light bar, a license plate decal facing backward, a cylindrical tow hitch, and a simple rear ladder with two rails and five rungs.

I'm skipping the spare tire since there's no good mounting spot, instead using that small rear deck gap for toolbox lockers, the ladder, and jerry cans. Now I'm positioning the exhaust stacks as vertical rods on either side, making sure they clear the pod's geometry.

Adding heat shields and glow rings to the stack tips, with brackets attaching to the back of the cab, then checking that the steer wheel fenders have enough clearance radius for turning. For the underglow strips, I'm figuring out placement along the skirt's bottom edge so they're visible beneath the hanging body panels.

I'm also thinking through some cyberpunk flourishes — a neon signage texture reading something like "CONVOY 7" on the locker side, and considering a hologram effect using an alpha-cutout textured plane rather than true transparency, maybe styled as a glowing cargo manifest or shield tag near the pod front.

I'll skip the floating holo card to keep things simple, but I still want sweeping catmull-curve cables for umbilical hoses, a coiled turret-to-roof cable, and deck-side cable runs. I'm adding a rear whip antenna with a spike base and a lathe-built dish on the roof, plus an amber spinning beacon atop the pod made from a base cylinder and a glowing half-sphere. Roughly tallying parts now — wheels around 48, axles near 40, frame pieces about 20.

Adding up the rest of the sections now — decks, pod, cab, turret, rear, and misc — I'm landing near 330 parts total, within budget but needing care with the triangle count given tori and many cylinders, so I'll keep the merged wheel geometry low-poly. Now I'm setting up the import statements for the three.js builder utilities, pulling in the paint, noise, and glow helpers along with the clockwork metal kit, double-checking that these all come from the single root module as the SDK convention dictates.

Mapping out remaining imports...

Drafting the AEGIS//HALCYON emblem SVG with a hex shield motif in magenta and cyan tones...

Now I'm designing a label badge with a dark hazard-striped background, bold "SEALED CARGO" text, a lot number with biohazard code, and a barcode graphic underneath.

Adding screen readout...

Now I'm sketching out the other panel textures: a dark grille with magenta slits, a teal/black visor with HUD glints and reticle lines, an amber stencil door number reading "CV-07," and a plate with text like "AEG 7741." I'm also planning a chevron-striped livery pattern in magenta/cyan/yellow to run along the cab's lower body and doors.

I'm reworking placement since fender flares block parts of the lower cab side, so I'm shifting the chevron decal elsewhere, like onto the bumper, and also considering a small neon sign decal reading something like "SEAL//7" for the locker side.

Now I'm writing the tyre geometry, generating a ring of tread blocks positioned around the cylinder's circumference, rotating each block by its angle so the radial, axial, and tangential dimensions align correctly with the wheel's local axes.

Staggering the two rows with a half-step offset gives 24 merged tread blocks per wheel. Now I'm sizing the rim cylinder slightly proud of the tyre profile so it reads as a distinct outer face detail.

I'm adding the hubcap details: a dark inner disc, a thin glowing neon ring rotated to face outward, and a set of six small lug-nut cylinders arranged in a circle, all merged in a local frame before being rotated into position depending on which side of the car the wheel sits on.

Now I'm planning the merged geometries for the wheel assembly: a tyre piece combining carcass and tread in rubber, and a separate rim piece with the hub cylinder, lip ring, and bolts in a metallic finish.

Skipping spokes and brake caliper details for simplicity. For the neon ring, I'm building a thin torus rotated so its axis points vertically, positioned at the rim's center, with a glowing material applied to the same placement.

Setting up helper functions for mirroring left/right parts and placing bones with rods and shapes...

Writing the edge-plate helper that computes normal vectors and rotation angle for placing panels along a line...

Verifying the rotation math: checking that the atan2 angle correctly maps the Y-axis to the edge direction and the local Z-axis to the perpendicular offset direction.

For the windscreen case, I compute the angle from its dz/dy components and confirm the resulting normal points outward correctly. Then I check the roof traversal front-to-back, verifying the -90° rotation gives a normal pointing straight up, and confirm the box texturing orientation keeps +X as right and +Y along the slope as expected.

Setting up color palette and metadata...

Writing grime color function...

Writing panel grid logic...

I'm estimating texture resolution against painted surface area to make sure seam widths stay proportionate—around 250 m² at 2048 resolution gives roughly a 9mm texel, so a 14mm seam works fine. I'm also deciding tire and hazard paint details stay as flat colors, then moving on to drafting the SVG strings for the build, including a trefoil path.

Writing SVG code for the trefoil symbol...

Now I'm defining a `makeTextures()` function to return the texture objects, and working out decal placement near the vehicle surface with positioning and sizing parameters. I'm also setting up the cab door joints for left and right sides.

Writing door geometry...

Still placing door and chassis details...

Now I'm adding mirror arms and camera pods extending from the door front, then sketching the cab roof plate with a slight slope.

Writing roof rib layout code...

Now I'm sketching the turret assembly: a bolted ring base at the chassis roof, with a yaw body cylinder sitting above it and a pitch joint positioned slightly higher and forward for the gun mount.

Still placing turret geometry... working out slanted side armor cheek plates, a gun cradle box, and twin barrel rods extending forward over the hood with shroud cylinders near the base and a muzzle brake at the tip.

Adding ammo boxes beside the yaw body with belt links sweeping to the cradle, a sensor pod with glowing lens on top, then shifting to cab details like a front bumper box positioned so it tucks under the nose without overlapping it.

Now I'm laying out the bumper's hazard paint and forward-facing spikes, considering a skid plate and tow hooks, then roughing in the headlight housings with glowing lens inserts on each side.

Still placing more details... adding brow plates over the headlights, fog lamps with cyan glow, a winch cylinder, and starting to plan the hood intake scoop geometry.

Now I'm figuring out the windscreen frame structure using edge-spanning helper segments for the bottom bar, top bar, glass, and side pillars, plus an angled brow visor above the glass, and sketching in a small glowing rear window slit on the cab's back panel.

Since the pod largely conceals the rear, I'm adding minor rear details like cable ports and umbilicals, then a roof-mounted light bar with alternating magenta/cyan/amber glow segments, beacon lamps, a roof hatch, and a sensor dome with antenna dish. I'm skipping the interior and moving on to underglow/neon elements, pod front/back detailing, and textured side lockers on the deck.

For the rigging, I'm defining wheel and turret hinge roles while keeping joint parenting explicit rather than relying on nearest-match defaults, making sure hinge directions and points are specified correctly for doors and other moving parts. I'm also working out glow application for sweep-based parts and routing a hose/umbilical curve connecting a port on the cab's back panel to a port on the pod's front cap, adjusting the connection points to match their actual positions.

I'm figuring out the sweep helper's signature for the hose geometry, confirming that color comes right after radius for sweep along with rod, capsule, spike, and sprout, then working out how to place ring details along the hose path using the along helper with the correct frame and bone parameters.

For the strap loop sweep, I'm trying to pin down which section axis maps to width versus depth — whether the binormal runs along z or radially around the pod, since that determines how the loop profile is oriented.

Rather than risk a flat blade-like strap from mismatched radii, I decide to just use equal rx=ry for a round rope-like cross section, sweeping an octagonal chain shape that's safe regardless of orientation ambiguity. I'm settling on a single round ratchet cable with a buckle box for a cyber-styled tie-down look.

Now I'm checking that surface.loop works correctly against a plane through a given point facing a direction, confirming it can target a lathe-built Part like the pod and extract its triangle loop even at mid-z sections. I move on to planning the pod's band rings as torus parts, then start detailing the rear seal lock: a flat disc cap at the back, with a large lock plate cylinder rotated to sit flush against the rear face.

I'm laying out the rest of the lock assembly — a glowing red ring torus, a trefoil-shaped plane oriented to face backward, four latch arm boxes spaced 90° apart around the cap radius with rotations to match their angular position, plus small glowing lamp spheres and a keypad plate positioned just below the lock, checking that its size and offset keep it from clashing with the lock plate's radius.

Now I'm skipping the keypad on the rear cap and focusing that side on the lock plus a label decal instead, then moving to the front cap where I'm placing a screen plane, keypad, and umbilical port cylinders with glow rings, plus small seal clamp boxes to bridge the visible gap between the cab and pod, and finally positioning logo and label decals along the pod's side within its mid-section z-range.

Now I'm placing the hazard triangle stickers and finalizing decal positions for the logos, labels, and screen on both sides of the pod, then adding half-torus handrail loops as lifting lugs on the pod roof using upright ring geometry at the top corners.

Next I'm adding vent stack boxes, a joint beacon with a glowing amber half-sphere and reflector near the top, and a thin cyan glow strip running along the top ridge, checking heights so it sits just above the roof face without poking through.

With the greebles settled, I'm moving on to the rear telemetry mast whip antenna and double-checking the triangle budget stays reasonable given the lathe segment count. Now I'm starting to assemble the final TypeScript code, importing the mesh utilities and procedural helpers needed, and confirming the part-building API handles shared geometry and positioning correctly before writing out the complete scene construction.

Defining a part-placement helper...

Setting up axle positions...

Next I'm looping over the axle array to place axles, diffs, and springs, then computing the fender arch outline as a z-y point sequence and extruding it along the x-axis at the wheel's offset position, attached to the chassis with proper thickness and color.

Now I'm checking whether the arch's y baseline aligns with the wheel hub height so the arc sits correctly, and considering adding a thin neon glow ring along the arch using a half-torus rotated to lie in the wheel's plane.

Adding a front prow armor wedge for detail. Time to commit to the full code now, keeping it to a reasonable scope while writing the texture generation functions, starting with the logo SVG.

Writing screen display SVG...

Finishing the label text with hazard details and barcode, then planning to generate all textures through an array map covering logo, label, screen, trefoil, hazard triangle, grille, visor, door number, plate, sign, and chevrons — eleven textures total.

Writing visor gradient and glint...

Also confirming the opaque base rect means the overlay polygons stay fully opaque after compositing, so the plane's texture layering holds up.

Now I'm building the tyre geometry by merging a cylinder core with tread blocks arranged radially around it, checking that the block thickness keeps the outer radius just past the wheel's base radius.

Writing rim geometry...

Still working out wheel geometry...

Still writing frame code...

Adding locker latches and hazard stripe details...

Adding handle, number plate, and glow accents to the door, including a cyan neon strip beneath the window and along the front edge, plus mirror arms and cab roof storage details. Checking that the joint syntax with directional vectors is correct, then I'm ready to finalize the output.
